newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's Patten dismisses Asian values as myth.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's Patten dismisses Asian values as myth.

text.p: The 28th and last British Governor of Hong Kong Chris Patten challenged the concept of Asian values and said a convergence of economic success and political liberalism was inevitable.
Patten made his comments in an essay contributed to the British magazine The Economist received here on Friday.

"To talk of Asian values requires one to explain away the differences between democracy in India and market Leninism in China; between a free press in the Philippines and Hong Kong and a controlled media in other places; between corruption in many Asian countries and clean government in Singapore," he wrote.

Patten whose five-year tenure draws to a close when the British colony of Hong Kong reverts to China on June 30, 1997, took issue with the notion of Confucian disciplines and the idea firm government was required to ensure economic growth.
"This argument is put with bullying panache by some leaders of an authoritarian disposition to justify the curbs on the freedoms of those they rule."

Patten, who provoked Chinese fury by spearheading democratic reforms in Hong Kong in the twilight of British rule, argued that as people grew prosperous, travelled and communicated more, they would demand greater say in decisions taken in their name.
"A more accountable and participative government is invariably the consequence sooner or later of economic growth and the opening of markets," he said.
He added there were lessons the West could learn from Asia.
"It defies reason and experience to pretend that public spending and tax levels have nothing to do with Asian success or European problems," he wrote.
But he urged commentators to maintain a sense of proportion -- it was free trade and access to European and North American markets which gave Asian economies their big break.
He advocated maintaining as much as possible a separation between trade and politics in the interests of free trade.

"If we are not to mix them up, then we should not permit Asian countries to play the same game in reverse, threatening that access to their markets can only be allowed to the politically correct, to those prepared to be muzzled over human rights."
